A1

Map-first Decision Dashboard  RECOMMENDED

The builder opens a map of Jordan and works from the land outward. This matches how builders actually think — they start with an area, not a form. It is the most natural fit for the "where should I build?" question, and it keeps every number in its real-world context.

Screen by screen

1
Open the map
the whole country at a glance

A full map of Jordan loads with an opportunity heatmap on top. Warmer areas = stronger build opportunity. Layer toggles let the builder add points of interest, roads, land use, or (recommended) a satellite / 3D-terrain layer.

2
Read the heatmap & click an area
"which area?"

The builder clicks a strong area (say Abdoun). A panel slides in with its Investment Score broken into dimensions (Market Potential, Demand, Competition, Future Growth, Infrastructure, Regulatory Readiness, Pricing Confidence) and an overall score — so areas can be ranked before any pricing.

3
See its intelligence (readiness)
"is it feasible? who buys here?"

The panel shows feasibility (zoning/rules, with gaps honestly labelled "data being enriched"), demand signals, and the comparable listings that will anchor the price — each with its source.

4
Evaluate a project
enter the plot

The builder enters buildable area, floors and finish level. The platform computes the maximum land price (residual land value) — what they can pay for the land and still hit their margin — using the official construction-cost floor.

5
Get the launch price
the defensible band

A launch-price band (minimum-safe / recommended / premium) with a decomposed confidence and a fully sourced adjustment waterfall — each line traceable to real listings.

6
Run what-if scenarios
stress-test the decision

20 floors instead of 10; construction cost +15%; the metro delayed two years; a later launch — every number updates live, so the builder sees how robust the plan is before committing capital.

7
Get the sales story
"justify it"

An auto-generated executive summary and plain-English sales narrative — ready for a board or a customer.

Why geographic-first fits builders

Land is geographic. A builder's first instinct is "which area?", and a map answers that instantly — then feasibility, market, economics and price all open in context around the place they picked. A form-first tool would force them to know the answer before they start; a map lets them explore and compare.

What building it out fully involves

  • Wire the opportunity heatmap to the live Investment Score across covered areas
  • Add the satellite & 3D-terrain layers that power the view/terrain factors
  • Connect the click-through panel to the pricing engine and the residual-land calculator
  • Build the what-if scenario controls on top of the engine
  • Performance-tune the map for large data (tens of thousands of listings)

Strengths

  • Matches how builders think — area first
  • Most exploratory — great for comparing places
  • The opportunity heatmap is front and centre
  • Everything stays in spatial context
  • Satellite / 3D layers plug straight into the terrain & view analysis

Trade-offs

  • A map-heavy screen needs good performance on large data
  • Slightly more to learn than a single search box
  • Best on a larger screen (desktop / tablet)
  • Satellite / 3D layers may add a small map cost
